title: Dead Space versus PaCO2 and the PaCO2 - EtCO2 Gap
subtitle: Observe how changes in physiological dead space fraction influence alveolar ventilation, carbon dioxide clearance, and end-tidal values

patient.summary: Intubated patient receiving mechanical ventilation with continuous capnography monitoring following orthopedic surgery.

prediction.question: When alveolar dead space fraction increases from 0.10 to 0.45 at constant ventilator settings, how will arterial PaCO2, end-tidal CO2 (EtCO2), and arterial pH change over the observation period?

whatToLookAtHint: Compare arterial PaCO2 from the blood gas with end-tidal CO2 on the capnogram, noting the size of the PaCO2 - EtCO2 difference.

reflection.question: Why does an increase in alveolar dead space fraction cause arterial PaCO2 to rise while end-tidal CO2 (EtCO2) paradoxically falls?

options.text: Alveolar ventilation drops so CO2 accumulates in blood, while unperfused ventilated alveoli dilute expired gas with CO2-free air.
CO2 production (VCO2) falls sharply due to impaired alveolar capillary diffusion.
The capnograph sensor malfunctions in the presence of increased physiological shunt.
High dead space causes metabolic alkalosis, which shifts the hemoglobin-CO2 dissociation curve.

reflection.explanation: Alveolar dead space consists of alveoli that are ventilated but underperfused (high V/Q). Because these alveoli do not participate in gas exchange, their gas contains virtually zero CO2. During exhalation, this CO2-free gas mixes with gas from perfused alveoli, lowering the mixed alveolar and end-tidal PCO2. Simultaneously, effective alveolar ventilation (VA = VE × (1 - VD/VT)) falls, impairing overall CO2 clearance and causing arterial PaCO2 to rise, markedly widening the PaCO2 - EtCO2 difference.

evidence.claim: Increased alveolar dead space impairs carbon dioxide elimination, elevating arterial PaCO2 while lowering mixed expired and end-tidal CO2, increasing the arterial-to-end-tidal CO2 difference.
evidence.source: Nuckton TJ, et al. Pulmonary dead-space fraction as a risk factor for death in the acute respiratory distress syndrome. N Engl J Med. 2002;346(17):1281-1286.

evidence.claim: Alveolar dead space produces dilution of alveolar gas by unperfused ventilated units, reducing EtCO2 relative to PaCO2.
evidence.source: Verscheure S, et al. Volumetric capnography: physiology and clinical applications. Curr Opin Crit Care. 2016;22(3):216-221.
